item.title: Once Home to Batman, This Faded Mansion Is Now Plagued by Real Bats
item.description:
Christian Bale once stalked its grounds as Batman, plotting his caped crusade from its recesses.

But the stately English home that featured in Christopher Nolan’s 2005 film “Batman Begins” has lately hosted another type of bat: the smaller and smellier kind.

Mentmore Towers, the 19th-century Jacobethan estate that served as Wayne Manor and as a backdrop for other movies, was found littered with bat droppings during an inspection by local environmental officials last year. They also found a dead bat.

Spooked by its decline, the authorities in Buckinghamshire, in the countryside northwest of London, are demanding that Mentmore’s owners carry out urgent bat surveys and roof repairs. If not, the officials said, they could move to force the owners to sell the mansion, which holds a Grade I listing, Britain’s highest heritage status.

“Our focus and priority is making sure this Grade I-listed building — well known and well-loved in Buckinghamshire — is protected and preserved,” Peter Strachan, the deputy leader of the local council, said this month.

Conservationists describe the 250-room manor as one of Britain’s finest examples of Jacobethan Revival architecture, an amalgam of Elizabethan and Jacobean styles.

It has been owned by the family trust of the British Syrian property tycoon Simon Halabi since 1998. The local officials gave Mr. Halabi’s family trust a deadline of Oct. 4 to comply with its repair notice and conduct professional bat surveys.

At least two species of bat appeared to be roosting in Mentmore Towers, local inspectors said, based on the droppings found there. The inspectors shared photographs of broken windows, ceiling holes and cracked exterior walls, which they said had offered the bats possible entry routes.

Bats are a protected species in Britain and property owners are legally obligated to take precautions to avoid disturbing them.

In response to the notice, Mr. Halabi’s family said that it had begun a bat survey and a program of repairs and restorations.

“There is an irony in the suggestion that nobody is dealing with the bats when a team of professional ecologists, effectively Mentmore’s own ‘Batman’ team, has already been on the case,” it said in a statement. The Halabi family trust was “absolutely committed to the long-term preservation and restoration of Mentmore Towers,” it added.

The statement argued that Buckinghamshire Council had slowed down the family’s efforts by opposing the construction of a security fence and a storage facility on the grounds. The council said they breached planning rules.

Mentmore Towers is the only major surviving work in Britain by Joseph Paxton, a Victorian innovator best known for designing London’s Crystal Palace, an iron-and-glass symbol of the Industrial Age that burned down in 1936.

Long before it was a filming location — including for Stanley Kubrick’s “Eyes Wide Shut” (1999), the Sacha Baron Cohen comedy “Ali G Indahouse” (2002) and the Spice Girls’ “Goodbye” music video — Mentmore served for over a century as a country palace of the Rothschild banking dynasty.

At one point it was home to a future British prime minister, the Earl of Rosebery, who married into the family. Photographs taken in 1975 show its grand hall dripping in tapestries, with lavish furnishings and a cabinet brimming with trophies.

Hit by British inheritance taxes nearing $7 million in the 1970s, the Rothschild family sold the house and held a flash auction of its furnishings. Over nine days in 1977, nearly 3,000 items of Baroque art, gilded furniture and other treasures were sold, fetching more than $10 million.

The following year, Mentmore was acquired by an organization that promoted transcendental meditation, according to a local history museum. Two decades later, Mr. Halabi’s family trust purchased the property with the idea of converting it into a luxury hotel.

According to court documents filed this month in a separate dispute between Mr. Halabi and a neighbor, the businessman said he ended up keeping the property as a family home after the death in 2003 of his eldest son, who was buried on the estate.

Mr. Halabi has been a fixture in the British news media for years. In the early 2000s, The Times of London named him one of Britain’s wealthiest people, having amassed a portfolio of properties that included a share in the development of the Shard, London’s tallest building. According to public records, he declared bankruptcy in 2010.

Historic England, the government’s heritage adviser, lists Mentmore Towers as a building of “exceptional interest,” a classification that requires owners to protect its architectural significance. The body now says the building is in a “very bad” state and requires urgent repair.

Constructed from 1852 to 1854 in buff sandstone, and noted for its large plate-glass windows, Mentmore took inspiration from Wollaton Hall, an Elizabethan mansion in the city of Nottingham, according to conservationists.

Morgan Ellis Leah, a conservationist at Britain’s Victorian Society, a heritage group, said that the pace of the building’s deterioration was deeply concerning.

“What remains of Mentmore’s interiors are of extraordinary quality: from the Caen stone entrance hall to the 12-meter-high grand hall with its glazed ceiling,” Mr. Leah said.

He commended local officials for trying to safeguard the mansion’s future, but added that the effort “underscores the fragility of the building and the absolute necessity of protecting its setting from further harm.”

item.title: Elaine Mokhtefi, American Witness to Algeria’s Revolution, Dies at 98
item.description:
Late one night in June 1969, Elaine Mokhtefi, a journalist with the Algerian government news service, received a call from a representative of the Zimbabwe African People’s Union, a militant group fighting the white-supremacist government of Southern Rhodesia.

He needed help. Eldridge Cleaver, a leader of the Black Panther Party, had jumped bail on an attempted murder charge in California, fled to Cuba and was now hiding in Algiers, the capital. Could she lean on her contacts in the Algerian government to arrange a visa?

African guerrillas, American radicals, top Algerian officials — Ms. Mokhtefi was used to it. What was strange was how she got there.

Born Elaine Klein in Brooklyn and educated in Georgia, she improbably found herself as an indispensable fixer for the Algerian independence movement in the 1950s and, after it separated from France in 1962, for the young Algerian republic, connecting its leaders with the revolutionaries and rebels who saw Algeria as a beacon for developing-world freedom movements.

“In the ’60s, we had the impression that what we did could have an impact,” Ms. Mokhtefi told Publishers Weekly in 2018. “We felt that we were on the edge of a new world.”

Ms. Mokhtefi died on Sept. 11 in Manhattan. She was 97.

The death, in a hospital, was confirmed by Zeynep Çelik, a neighbor and close friend.

After dropping out of college and moving to Paris in 1951, Ms. Mokhtefi became drawn to the plight of Algerian workers, who faced constant discrimination, and to their homeland’s smoldering campaign for independence from France, which broke out into full-scale war in 1954.

By decade’s end, she was working for the provisional Algerian government, first in Paris and later in New York, helping its officials navigate the United Nations and cultivate ties with the U.S. government.

Fluent in French, she proved adept at moving between cultures and causes, helping link the Algerian struggle to the broader fight against European colonialism in Africa and Asia.

Following independence, Ms. Mokhtefi moved to Algiers, where she continued her work as a fixer.

She met Fidel Castro in Cuba. She hosted North Korean delegates in Algiers. She was close friends with Frantz Fanon, the Martinican-born French psychiatrist and writer, and in 1961 took care of his son while Mr. Fanon lay dying of leukemia in a Maryland hospital.

In 1969, she was a lead organizer of the Pan-African Cultural Festival in Algiers. At one point, she and the South African singer Miriam Makeba had to cajole, threaten and finally carry a very drunk Nina Simone from her hotel room to the stage, where she sang songs that brought Houari Boumédiène, the Algerian president, nearly to tears.

Ms. Mokhtefi had a cameo in Gillo Pontecorvo’s acclaimed 1966 film “The Battle of Algiers,” a cinéma-vérité depiction of the Algerian war of independence; she appears at a news conference held by a French officer.

She was in Algeria in 1970 when Timothy Leary, the American psychologist and counterculture celebrity, escaped to the country after breaking out of prison in California, where he was being held on a drug conviction. She arranged for him and his wife, Rosemary, to meet with government officials and stay in Algiers.

And she was the main point of contact between the Algerian government and Mr. Cleaver, arranging for him, his wife and his associates — eventually about 30 Panthers — to receive something like diplomatic status in Algeria, which included a stipend and the use of a villa outside Algiers.

The Panthers added to Algeria’s mystique as an international center for revolutionaries, but their flashy American lifestyle raised eyebrows among what was, still, a conservative Muslim country.

One day Mr. Cleaver confessed a secret to Ms. Mokhtefi: He had killed one of his close associates, Clinton Smith, known as Rahim. He said the man had been trying to steal from the Panthers. Ms. Mokhtefi later learned that Mr. Smith had been seen dancing closely with Mr. Cleaver’s wife at a disco while he had been on a trip to North Korea, and she suspected the killing had a different motivation.

Mr. Cleaver was never charged in the killing.

By the early 1970s, Ms. Mokhtefi had begun to turn against Algeria’s increasingly repressive government. She refused a request by government agents to spy on a close friend, a transgression that got her expelled from the country in 1974. She later lived in Paris and New York City.

“She remained cleareyed about the authoritarian nature of the post-independence regime,” Adam Shatz, a writer who befriended her in 2014, said in an interview. “But she retained an abiding love for the country.”

Elaine Klein was born on Dec. 10, 1928. Her parents, Charlie and Mildred Klein, owned a dry goods store in Hempstead, a Long Island suburb, but it failed at the onset of the Great Depression in 1929.

The family moved repeatedly, first back to the city from Long Island, then to Texas, then to upstate New York and finally to Ridgefield, Conn., an experience that established Elaine’s comfort with different surroundings and affinity for outsiders.

She attended Wesleyan College, a women’s institution in Macon, Ga., but was expelled after a year for speaking out against Jim Crow segregation and for breaking curfew to visit Atlanta on the weekends.

Back in New York, she studied Spanish and became active in the United World Federalists, a left-wing group that advocated for world government. Her involvement led to surveillance by the F.B.I., and was one reason she moved to Paris in 1951.

There, she fell in with the left-wing political and artistic scene, including the Algerian independence movement. Eventually she returned to New York to represent the Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic, working out of a small office near the United Nations.

She did not visit Algeria until after its independence. For more than a decade, she was the only American and among the only women working at a high level within the government.

Her expulsion in 1974 stung. By then she had fallen in love with a former freedom fighter, Mokhtar Mokhtefi, who left with her. They lived for 20 years in Paris, where she sold jewelry, and married in 1991. They moved in 1994 to New York City, where she became an accomplished painter.

She also became involved in various protest movements, and was a regular presence at demonstrations against the Iraq War and for Palestinian rights.

Mr. Mokhtefi died in 2015. Ms. Mokhtefi does not leave any immediate survivors.

Just after his death, Mr. Mokhtefi’s memoir was published in French; Ms. Mokhtefi translated it into English and published it as “I Was a French Muslim” in 2021. By then she had also published her own memoir, “Algiers, Third World Capital: Freedom Fighters, Revolutionaries, Black Panthers” in 2018.

The book, which Mr. Shatz helped arrange for publication, was well received and won her acclaim on the left. Despite her age — she was 90 when it appeared — she took to the road for speaking tours, including visits to Algeria, whose new democratic government welcomed her openly.

She received Algerian citizenship in July of this year. At her death, she was finalizing plans to visit Algiers again in October, where she was to receive an award from the government.

item.title: U.N. General Assembly Set to Snarl Traffic, City Leaders Say
item.description:
Representatives from nearly 200 countries will descend on New York City this week as leaders converge on Midtown East in Manhattan for the annual session of the United Nations General Assembly, bringing motorcades — and therefore, traffic — with them.

“I know that, for many New Yorkers, the General Assembly is more synonymous with questions around traffic,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference last week. “When the world visits New York City, our streets are inevitably impacted.”

In addition to planned street closures for the entire week, there will also be rolling closures as delegations travel across the city.

Here’s what you need to know:

Midtown!

There are no known specific threats to this year’s General Assembly, Jessica Tisch, the police commissioner, said. Still, officers will secure hundreds of motorcades as heads of state and high-ranking officials move between hotels, U.N. buildings and meetings around the city.

“This is one of the most complex security operations that we carry out,” she said. “As always, there will be security measures that you will see and others that you will not see.”

A gridlock alert is in place from Sept. 21 to Sept. 25, Mr. Mamdani said. Rolling pedestrian and vehicle closures will take place around the United Nations Headquarters, spilling out across the city as delegations traverse the city. Portions of F.D.R. Drive will be closed, and ferry service will be disrupted, the mayor said.

Closed to vehicles

All day

Sept. 20–26

MANHATTAN

E. 47th St.

E. 48th St.

E. 46th St.

2nd Ave.

E. 45th St.

United Nations

Headquarters

1st Ave.

E. 44th St.

E. 42nd St.

East River

Closed to vehicles

Until 9 p.m.

Sept. 20–26

Edison Wu/The New York Times

Ms. Tisch said that from Sept. 20 through Sept. 26, First Avenue will be closed between 41st and 48th Streets, while 44th Street to 47th Street will be closed between First and Second Avenues. Each day until the end of the session, around 9 p.m., 42nd Street will close between First and Second Avenues.

The 42nd Street exit from F.D.R. Drive will also be blocked off. The Police Department said closures on parts of the F.D.R. will occur as needed.

The mayor recommended that commuters use public transportation.

“I want to thank New Yorkers in advance for their patience,” Mr. Mamdani said.

Each year, there is an uptick in protests related to the General Assembly, Ms. Tisch said. Those protests are generally contained to Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza on East 47th Street, but can grow to affect other parts of the city.

This year, protests are planned throughout the week, including demonstrations at Bryant Park, at Union Square and in Brooklyn.

“As always, the N.Y.P.D. will facilitate First Amendment activity,” Ms. Tisch said. “At the same time, there will be no tolerance for violence or destruction of property.”

item.title: An Unused and Divisive Philippine Nuclear Plant Awaits Its Fate
item.description:
Noel Germano leads the way through the dark, airless hallways of the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant, an isolated compound west of Manila that was meant to be the first source of atomic energy in the Philippines. Instead of the thrum of massive turbines and steam generators, there is eerie silence: The plant has been mothballed for decades.

A yellow radiation protection suit is only for display, unneeded by Mr. Germano, who manages the plant, or any of his seven engineers as they go about the Sisyphean task of manually turning thousands of analog dials, switches and gears to prevent decay.

The plant was heralded by President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. in the 1970s as a step into a prosperous, modern era for the Philippines. Of its four planned reactors, only one unit was completed, in 1984, and it was never switched on. Decades later, his son — who was elected president in 2022 — has revived the country’s pursuit of atomic energy and his government is exploring options including potentially reviving the plant in Bataan.

The hulking concrete structure sits on an 800-acre site fenced off from the small seaside town of Morong. The plant’s grounds are still well maintained, but its interior, with the reactor that was designed to produce 621 megawatts, resembles a museum diorama. Bringing it to life is not impossible, but it is a tall and expensive ask, experts say.

The goal is the same now as it was in the ’70s: energy security. The elder Marcos, a dictatorial leader who was in power from 1965 to 1986, wanted to diversify the Philippines’ energy sources to guard against global oil shocks like the one in 1973. His son, Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr., has had to deal with similar fallout from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Reviving the Bataan plant might prove a hard sell in a cash-strapped country, especially to the Filipinos who see it as a reminder of the corruption and repression of the Marcos Sr. era. And the threat of nuclear catastrophe feels immediate for many residents of Morong, about a mile up the coast.

The project has never been free of skepticism, facing a number of questions from the beginning: Does the Philippines have enough expertise to run a nuclear power plant safely? Is it wise to build one in a part of the world where earthquakes and tsunamis are a constant threat? Can the country even afford it?

The elder Mr. Marcos’ government managed to secure financing for the plant through debt. Hundreds of engineers and technicians were sent abroad for training to build up a work force capable of running a nuclear facility.

The site, on a peninsula across the bay from Manila, was chosen because there was abundant water to cool the reactor and it was considered high enough to be safe from tsunamis, a constant threat because of frequent earthquakes in the region.

Construction began in 1976, bringing a windfall for the many people in Morong and other nearby towns who were hired to work on the project. They included Valentino Tolosa, who said he could not believe his luck when, at the age of 18, he got a job as a cable puller. It paid about $27 a day, ten times the allowance he got from his mother, he said.

Three years into the plant’s construction, more than 8,000 miles away in Pennsylvania, a reactor at Three Mile Island suffered a partial meltdown in what remains the worst nuclear energy accident in U.S. history. It turbocharged the antinuclear movement in the Philippines, whose activists came to Morong regularly to campaign against the plant being built nearby.

Rumors also spread across the Philippines in the 1970s that the site was particularly dangerous because it sat above a fault line, and was less than 40 miles from Mount Pinatubo, an active volcano. Researchers from the Philippine Department of Science and Technology have since found no active fault lines under Bataan, and the site was unharmed by the volcano’s most destructive eruption in 1991.

The first Marcos government, which displayed little tolerance for dissent, came down hard on the plant’s opponents.

Pilar Nazareno, a resident of Morong, said dozens of her neighbors who had questioned the nuclear project at the time were taken by the police or labeled communists by the government. Some residents pretended to attend Bible studies at a local church as cover for discussions about the plant, she said.

“It fell to the priests and nuns to teach us about the nuclear plant, and what would happen to us if it had a meltdown,” said Ms. Nazareno, 68.

The Three Mile Island accident led the Philippine authorities to suspend construction at Bataan in 1979 for a safety review. The design was updated and work resumed the next year, but safety was just one of the criticisms: Mr. Marcos faced persistent allegations of corruption related to the project, including that the American company Westinghouse had given him millions of dollars in illegal payments to secure a contract to build the plant.

By the time it was completed in 1984, the plant’s cost had more than doubled to over $2 billion. It took another two decades for the government to pay off the accumulated debt.

Mr. Marcos by then was struggling for his political survival. In February 1986, he was overthrown and fled the country. With its biggest backer out of office, the nuclear plant’s future was thrown into doubt.

“When the government changed, we already knew nothing would move forward at the plant,” said Antonio Corpuz, a chemical engineer who was appointed the plant’s manager in 1978.

Two months after Mr. Marcos’ ouster, a reactor exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in the Soviet Union, in what became the world’s worst nuclear accident. It left little appetite in the Philippines for the Bataan project. A new government mothballed the plant in April that year, and sold its uranium fuel to other countries.

The site’s two backup generators were taken away to provide power to remote islands. Radiation detectors were also removed from the security posts because they were not needed: There was no nuclear material at the plant.

Mr. Corpuz and his team, instead of overseeing power generation, were tasked with preserving the plant. And in the 1990s, hundreds of engineers left after the government cut its maintenance budget, leaving only enough for a skeleton crew. Many went to the United States, Japan, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates for higher-paying jobs.

Today, the only part of the plant that appears pristine is the reactor room, a 164-foot-high cylindrical structure with steel-reinforced, three-foot-thick concrete walls. The structure protects the reactor core, which sits in a deep well that would be filled with water if the plant were operational. Many components in the core are still wrapped in plastic.

Supporters of the Bataan plant have pointed to reactors of the same design in the United States and South Korea that have run safely for decades.

Mark Cojuangco, a member of Congress and a champion of the Bataan plant, said the Philippines had missed an opportunity by mothballing the project. “We could have built factories like South Korea and leaped ahead of the region,” said Mr. Cojuangco, whose father was a tycoon close to Mr. Marcos Sr.

The younger Mr. Marcos has appeared mindful of the Bataan plant’s history and the long-running skepticism about its safety and usefulness, often avoiding direct mention of the project.

In 2024, his government commissioned a study by the Korea Hydro and Nuclear Power Company on the feasibility of reviving the plant. The Energy Department of the Philippines said in July that the study had been completed, but declined to provide its findings. A 2017 study by the same South Korean company found that about a quarter of the plant’s equipment would need to be replaced before it could be switched on, at a cost of about $1 billion.

Mr. Marcos had aimed for the Philippines to start generating nuclear power by 2032, but the Energy Department told reporters in July that it might take until 2038 as the agency evaluates other options, including plants at different sites. A 2024 survey commissioned by the Energy Department found more than 70 percent of Filipinos in favor of nuclear power.

If the government decides in favor of the Bataan plant, the refit is still expected to take years.

Mr. Germano, the plant’s manager, said he doubted he would see it switched on in his tenure. He retires in 2030.

item.title: Reported Explosions Put Saudi Capital on Edge Amid Conflict With Houthis
item.description:
Emergency alerts sounded in Saudi Arabia’s capital on Saturday as residents reported loud explosions and flights were disrupted at the city’s airport, further unnerving the country after days of escalating conflict between the kingdom and the Houthi militia in Yemen.

It was not immediately clear what had caused the explosions and the disruptions, and there were no immediate reports of casualties.

But the alerts were the first in the capital, Riyadh, in months, as the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have accused each other of mounting increasingly intense attacks in recent weeks. Attacks on Saudi Arabia have disrupted critical oil infrastructure and fueled alarm over threats to global energy supplies.

FlightRadar24, a flight tracking website, showed major delays on Saturday afternoon at the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Photographs and video by the Reuters news agency showed a plume of smoke rising in the vicinity of the airport.

The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday. There was no public comment from the Houthis, a group backed by Iran that has been at war with Yemen’s Saudi-backed government for over a decade.

Overnight, Riyadh residents received two emergency alerts warning of a “hostile aerial threat.” On Saturday, two booms rattled western Riyadh, home to a diplomatic quarter hosting foreign embassies. Saudi Civil Defense officials said early-warning systems were also activated in nine other cities.

It marked the first time alerts were sounded in Riyadh since tensions with the Houthis flared in July. Recent strikes had largely targeted southern Saudi cities, sparing the capital, where Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia is scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative, a major gathering of billionaires and international financiers, in October.

The Houthis and the internationally-recognized government of Yemen have been at war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. Soon after, Saudi Arabia led a bombing campaign to try to restore the government, plunging Yemen into a devastating civil war until a fragile truce was reached in 2022.

The reported explosions in Riyadh followed Houthi accusations on Friday that Saudi Arabia had attempted a “criminal” attack on Sanaa. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the group foiled the attacks, without detailing their nature.

On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia’s air defenses intercepted a Houthi drone approaching Mecca, the Saudi authorities said — a direct accusation that the militia had targeted Islam’s holiest site. Abdulmalik al-Houthi, the movement’s leader, dismissed the claim as “slander and fabrication.”

The Houthis also claimed on Wednesday that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Yemen’s Marib province last week using a locally made missile.

The hostilities are the most dangerous since the 2022 truce frayed. Fighting reignited in July after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. In response, the Houthis launched drone and ballistic missile barrages at Saudi military bases, ports, and airports, while targeting oil tankers in the Red Sea in what they called a naval blockade.

The Houthis have reported several Saudi air raids on their positions in several provinces. Domestic fighting in Yemen has also intensified following the Houthi capture of the country’s entire western Red Sea coastline, heightening risks for the Bab el-Mandab Strait, a vital global trade choke point.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen and Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from al-Mukalla, Yemen.

item.title: Israeli President Pardons Ex-Soldier Over Killing of Incapacitated Palestinian
item.description:
Israel’s president on Saturday expunged the criminal record of a former soldier who fatally shot a severely wounded Palestinian assailant a decade ago, fulfilling a long-sought demand from Israel’s right.

The case of the soldier, Elor Azaria, set off intense public debate in Israel and abroad in 2016 over Israeli soldiers’ treatment of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and whether Israel would prosecute members of the security forces accused of grave crimes.

Isaac Herzog, the Israeli president, said on Saturday that he had decided to clear Mr. Azaria’s criminal record after “examining all the circumstances of the case and the considerations related to the request,” and “after many years in which Azaria bore the consequences of his actions.”

Mr. Azaria was convicted of manslaughter for shooting the injured Palestinian man, Abdul Fattah al-Sharif, in Hebron, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. The episode, which was captured on video, began when Mr. al-Sharif and another man stabbed and wounded an Israeli soldier at a checkpoint. Israeli soldiers shot Mr. al-Sharif six times and killed the other attacker, and Mr. Azaria arrived at the scene about six minutes later.

After several more minutes, Mr. Azaria shot Mr. al-Sharif, 21, in the head at close range as he lay motionless on the ground — drawing condemnation from the Israeli military and resulting in a trial that exposed deep divisions in Israeli society. Mr. Azaria served nine months in prison and was released on parole.

The pardon by Mr. Herzog came amid a rising number of attacks by Jewish settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, and growing international condemnation of that violence. The president’s decision also immediately fueled speculation about why Mr. Herzog, who recently spoke out against “brutalization” creeping into Israeli society, would do such a thing, and whether he might be considering the politically contentious pardon of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the corruption charges he faces.

Mr. Herzog said that the decision was made “in the spirit of the season of mercy,” and because of Mr. Azaria’s “desire to remove the barriers currently standing in his way where employment is concerned and open a new chapter in his life.”

It was also based, he said, on “the complex medical circumstances the Azaria family has faced” and “changes that have taken place in Elor Azaria’s life since then,” without providing further detail.

The pardon highlighted the longstanding rifts within Israel, setting off intense criticism from human rights activists and opponents of Israel’s right-wing government, and celebrations from some of its most prominent leaders.

“On the eve of Yom Kippur, this is a correct, humane and fitting decision that expresses the spirit of forgiveness and the opportunity to turn over a new leaf,” the defense minister, Israel Katz, said in a statement. “Granting this pardon sends an important message” to Israeli soldiers and their families: “We do not abandon our soldiers, nor do we leave them behind,” he added.

Rights activists described the pardon as evidence supporting their accusations of a double standard for Israeli soldiers accused of crimes against Palestinians. Mr. Azaria was one of only a handful of Israeli soldiers to be convicted in recent years over the wrongful death of a Palestinian.

“The Azaria case marked a watershed moment, after which Israel’s political leadership and much of the public openly embraced the rejection of accountability,” said Ziv Stahl, the director of Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. “The president’s decision is a clear demonstration that the Israeli justice system is neither willing nor able to enforce the law against soldiers who harm Palestinians.”

Some analysts called the pardon a potential test by Mr. Herzog, who had led an opposition party before being elected president, as he weighs a push from the right to pardon Mr. Netanyahu. Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, made that call explicit on Saturday, calling on the president to pardon the prime minister as well.

Mr. Ben-Gvir also called on the Israeli chief of staff to allow Mr. Azaria, if he wants, “to return to the ranks” of the Israeli military.

item.title: Russia Barred Their Party, but These Antiwar Voices Are Still Standing
item.description:
They have almost no chance of winning. Their party, Yabloko, was formally removed from the nationwide ballot in this weekend’s elections. Their fellow party members have been sentenced to years in prison for their antiwar positions.

None of that is stopping them.

The fact that Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal opposition party, is fielding 98 candidates in 42 regions feels like a small miracle for antiwar Russians whom restrictive laws have prevented from openly expressing their views. As wartime repression deepens, the country may not see such candidates on the ballot again.

“There were times in Russian history that were worse,” said Grigory Grishin, a Yabloko candidate running for the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of Parliament, in Moscow. “So, as the saying goes, ‘The eyes are afraid, but the hands do the work’ — we are participating. What else is there to do?”

The fate of Yabloko has been the most consequential story line in an election the Kremlin engineered to be as uneventful as possible.

The party, long considered irrelevant by the Russian authorities, became a Kremlin target this summer after it unexpectedly turned into a vessel for antiwar sentiment. The Russian Supreme Court barred the party at the last minute, citing minor copyright infringements and indirect foreign financing that it said violated the law.

Still, the decision left open one avenue for Yabloko candidates to run.

At the ballot box, Russians choose a party and then a candidate from their district. Half of State Duma seats are filled through the party vote — parties must clear a 5 percent threshold — and the other half through the votes for candidates in districts, as in elections for the U.S. Congress.

While the Supreme Court barred Yabloko from the party-list vote, many of the party’s candidates in individual districts remained on the ballot. The authorities later disqualified them in many regions, but as voting began on Friday, nearly 100 were still standing.

Why they were allowed is unclear. There may not have been enough time to drum up cases against every one of them, analysts said. Or the authorities may feel confident that they have disqualified all of the Yabloko district candidates with a good chance of winning and that any unforeseen victories could be fixed with ballot falsifications.

Recent data from ExtremeScan, a Russian pollster, suggested that the authorities may have had reason to fear rising support for Yabloko, the only party running on an antiwar platform.

In a survey this month, 18 percent of respondents said they would have voted for Yabloko on a party-list ballot. It was a surprising figure for a party that has not cleared the threshold to enter the Duma since 1999. The idea that any Yabloko candidate would be allowed to take a seat in the legislature and use the platform to question the war openly is considered unthinkable in today’s Russia.

Aleksei Minyailo, an opposition activist in Moscow and the founder of the independent pollster Chronicles, said one of the most important steps that autocratic authorities took to shape election outcomes was limiting the field of candidates.

“This is the essential thing,” he said. “It’s more essential than who gets what result.”

The Kremlin could ultimately try to use the remaining Yabloko candidates to its advantage, Mr. Minyailo said, presenting a poor showing by them as evidence that antiwar Russians are a marginal minority.

In recent polling, the share of Russians who say they do not support the war has ranged from about 20 to 35 percent.

While the mere presence of Yabloko candidates on the ballot may be a victory for them, Mr. Grishin, the district candidate in Moscow, said it was always going to be an uphill battle.

The candidate running against him from the pro-Kremlin governing party, United Russia, had a budget that Mr. Grishin estimated at 40 million rubles, or $500,000. His own budget, raised through donations, was about one-tenth of 1 percent of that.

“We could only print 5,000 leaflets,” he said, proffering one with his portrait and a dove carrying an olive branch. It bore the party’s campaign slogan: “For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!”

Financial troubles were just one of Mr. Grishin’s worries. This month, a day after his newborn daughter arrived at home from the hospital, Mr. Grishin was detained and taken to a police station. He was later accused of “displaying extremist symbols,” a common pretext for removing candidates from the ballot. In Mr. Grishin’s case, the charge referred to a reference he had made on Telegram to the deceased opposition politician Aleksei A. Navalny, whom the Russian authorities branded an extremist.

Had the accusation come three months earlier, Mr. Grishin would have been automatically disqualified from running in the election. But because it occurred so late in the election cycle, the authorities could not remove him from the ballot.

Some candidates have been disqualified after parties loyal to the Kremlin brought cases against them. Iya Boronina, who leads Yabloko’s regional branch in the central Russian republic of Udmurtia, was barred after being accused of copyright infringement, echoing the case that the party itself faced in the Supreme Court.

Her campaign video featured the 1982 rock anthem “Bad to the Bone.” Representatives of the nationalist party A Just Russia contended that Ms. Boronina, because of sanctions against Russia, could not have paid in U.S. dollars for the legal right to use the song.

Eight Yabloko members are currently in prison for their antiwar stances. One deputy chairman, Maxim Kruglov, is serving a seven-year sentence, and another deputy, Lev Shlosberg, is serving 11 years.

Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai I. Rybakov, said that despite the harsh penalties faced by its leaders, the party had become a beacon for Russia’s youngest voters, who dislike the increasing government restrictions on the internet, speech and culture. More than 13,000 people applied to become party members during the election cycle, he said.

“They removed us from the election list because real support belongs to Yabloko, and they cannot defeat us in an election,” Mr. Rybakov said in an interview in his party’s library as his shelter dog, Morty, sat quietly by his side.

Mr. Rybakov pulled a book from the piles around him. It was Roberto Carnero’s essays on the gay Italian filmmaker and writer Pier Paolo Pasolini. About 15 percent of its words were blacked out. On some pages, only a few words were visible.

“The young people who come here are absolutely free people,” said Mr. Rybakov, who himself was disqualified from the election because of a post he wrote after Mr. Navalny died in prison in what five European countries said was a poisoning.

“They want nobody telling them what color their hair should be, what clothes to wear, what to say, what to think, who to love, where to work, or which professor to study with,” he added.

Several young people who attended Yabloko meetings spoke of the psychological solace of speaking with others who opposed the war.

Many of the questions Mr. Rybakov fielded addressed a growing rift between the opposition forces inside Russia centered around Yabloko and those forced into exile, including Mr. Navalny’s team. They have differed over the best strategy for voters to try to express discontent in the election.

As Mr. Rybakov was speaking on a recent night, news broke that another Yabloko candidate, Aleksandr Muravyov, had been barred from the election. Another party had filed a complaint alleging that Mr. Muravyov’s use of the slogan “For a free internet without blocks” created a negative image of other candidates and parties.

item.title: Hundreds of Drones Target Moscow on Final Day of Russian Elections
item.description:
Moscow and its surrounding region came under attack by hundreds of drones, the local authorities said on Sunday morning, killing two people and injuring 20.

About 1,600 drones heading toward the Moscow region were shot down, the Russian capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said, including 450 that had been approaching the city. An oil refinery and a warehouse were struck in the attack.

The attack came on the final day of parliamentary, regional and local elections across Russia. Russian officials have repeatedly said they are holding these votes under attack, possibly an implicit criticism of Ukraine, which has not held elections since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 because martial law forbids them. President Vladimir V. Putin has repeatedly criticized Kyiv and President Volodymyr Zelensky for not holding a vote.

Mr. Zelensky posted on Facebook that the bombardment included the first use of a newly developed Ukrainian ballistic missile to strike inside Russia. That missile does not have the range to reach Moscow, according to its manufacturer, Fire Point, so would have been aimed elsewhere in Russia.

The night was deadlier in Ukraine, where seven people were killed in strikes in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, according to Ukrainian authorities. Air alerts were on and off all night though most of the country.

Moscow’s mayor said “a few drones” struck the Moscow oil refinery in Kapotnya, which had been taken out of commission by attacks in June. At the time, it was estimated that the repairs would last for six months. On Sunday, Mr. Sobyanin said the refinery had again been damaged.

In the neighborhood of Ramenskoye, a 21-story building caught fire, and 600 residents were evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov.

A warehouse in the Moscow region was also struck, though no casualties were reported. For months, Ukraine has been targeting warehouses in Russia with long-range strikes.

All four airports in the Moscow region introduced temporary restrictions at the time of the attacks, and more than 30 flights were grounded, according to the newspaper Kommersant.

On Saturday, Mr. Sobyanin reported that a total of 2,022 drones had flown toward the Moscow region over the preceding seven days, 186 of which were shot down as they approached Moscow. Most of the drones had been shot down while they were still far from the city.

President Trump said last Monday that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to stop campaigns of pounding one another’s energy infrastructure but neither side has confirmed that an agreement had been reached. The attacks have continued through the week.

The outcome of the Russian elections looks to be a foregone conclusion: victory for the ruling party that supports Mr. Putin, because the Kremlin has engineered the vote to minimize competition.

Russians dread what may come after the Kremlin receives what most expect will be its desired result at the ballot box — whether that be another, albeit quieter, round of mobilization, more tax rises or more internet restrictions.

The country is already facing widespread fuel shortages because of Ukraine’s attacks on refineries. While fuel lines have become commonplace in the last few months, there were few on Saturday because not many fuel stations had any gas to sell. When they had something, it was low-quality gas or diesel.

In his statement on Facebook, Mr. Zelensky said the Ukrainians had struck with several types of domestically made drones and missiles created during the war in response to Russian missile attacks on Ukraine. These included Fury, FP-1 and Flamingo exploding drones, the Palianytsia cruise missile and the FP-7 Pelican ballistic missile, Mr. Zelensky said in the statement.

The Pelican missile is already in production in Ukraine, along with a larger, longer-range version expected to enter combat tests later this fall. The longer-range version, the FP-9, could reach Moscow.

item.title: Germans Are Voting Again, Amid a Far-Right Surge. Here’s What to Watch.
item.description:
Just two weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, scored a stunning victory in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, German voters in two other regions are voting on Sunday and will deliver a new gauge of the AfD’s national prospects.

Voters in Berlin and in a lightly populated coastal corner of the former East Germany, Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, will elect new state Parliaments on Sunday. The AfD is poised to gain significantly in both elections, even if polls suggest it will fall well short of its performance in Saxony-Anhalt, where it won 44 percent of the vote and could soon form a government.

The AfD’s leaders have used Nazi slogans and played down the significance of the Holocaust, and German intelligence has classified the party as a “suspected extremist” group. Yet it has harnessed voter anxiety over the economy and immigration, as well as the widespread unpopularity of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a mainstream conservative.

But surveys in the waning days of the campaign suggest Sunday’s vote could yet result in a backlash to the AfD’s rise. After leading in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania throughout the year, the AfD has now fallen into a virtual tie with the center-left Social Democrats.

In liberal Berlin, the AfD looks set to finish behind both Mr. Merz’s center-right Christian Democrats and the far-left party Die Linke.

Polls close at 6 p.m. in both areas. Here’s what to know.

Much of what fueled the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt is also present in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, a state of 1.5 million residents. Unemployment there is higher than the national average, as in Saxony-Anhalt. Residents still resent how eastern Germany struggled after the reunification of Germany in 1990. And many are sympathetic to Russia and wary of immigration, which surged in Germany during the European migration a decade ago.

Goldie Nickel, a young voter in the city of Neubrandenburg, said this past week that she supported the AfD because she felt the government wasn’t tough enough on immigrants.

“Migrants and refugees that either break the law or misbehave should be sent back to their home countries,” she said.

The AfD is only a co-favorite in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania because the state has a rarity for eastern Germany today: a popular leader from a mainstream party.

Manuela Schwesig, a Social Democrat, has governed the state since 2017 and has campaigned vigorously to keep her job. She has at times distanced herself from her national party leaders, who are the junior partners in Mr. Merz’s federal coalition government, and built an independent brand with voters.

As the state premier, Ms. Schwesig has said clearly what she intends to do — and follows through on those promises, said Bettina Müller, also of Neubrandenburg. Her vote for the Social Democrats on Sunday, she said, would be for Ms. Schwesig personally.

The Social Democrats may be bolstered by center-right voters who hope to deny the AfD first place, said William Thay, the president of Le Millénaire, a French think tank tracking the race. “In Mecklenburg, we believe we have strategic voters,” he said. “They will vote against the AfD.”

In Germany’s capital, the far-left Die Linke party is surging after a campaign dominated by the price and scarcity of urban housing.

Die Linke has campaigned on an initiative to take public ownership of 270,000 apartments owned by private real estate giants, in a bid to make housing more plentiful and affordable. “We want an end to speculation with our homes,” said Elif Eralp, the party’s mayoral candidate, on her Instagram.

Pre-election polls show Die Linke could win the election, in what would be a first for Berlin. Die Linke supporters see parallels between Ms. Eralp, born in Munich to two left-wing activists from Turkey, and Zohran Mamdani, the leftist mayor of New York.

Yet even if Die Linke comes first, it could struggle to form a coalition government. The Social Democrats and the center-left Greens may decide to partner with the Christian Democrats, who are Die Linke’s closest rivals in the race.

The AfD is projected to come in third in Berlin, a result that would keep it from joining the city’s coalition government because the other parties consider it extremist.

Bad results for the Christian Democrats in both elections could further imperil the unpopular chancellor, particularly in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, which is being more closely watched. Many in his party blamed Mr. Merz for the size of the AfD win in Saxony-Anhalt.

Mr. Merz’s party is polling in single digits in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania. If it fails to reach the 5 percent threshold for representation in the state Parliament, it would notch a postwar low for the party and amplify calls in Berlin for Mr. Merz to step aside.

The odds of that scenario are low, Mr. Thay said, but not impossible.

Tatiana Firsova contributed reporting from Berlin, and Philip Kaleta from Neubrandenburg, Germany.

]]>

item.title: Israeli Tourist Trap ‘Herod’s Pool’ Is Draining Palestinians’ Land Dry
item.description:
On a hot August morning in the West Bank’s desert, an Israeli teenager performed a backflip into the cool water of an ancient reservoir. It was filled with water diverted from Palestinians’ farms.

The farmers used to grow watermelons, eggplants and cucumbers in the arid Jordan Valley. But in June, their main irrigation source — a pipeline that brought spring water to their crops and a surrounding community — was severed and redirected to the reservoir, according to the farmers and the Israeli military.

During a visit last month, water gushed from the pipe into the pool, where dozens of Israelis were splashing around while others picnicked nearby, trespassing on private land.

“One morning nothing came out of the pipe,” said Saad Nemer, a soft-spoken 69-year-old farmer, who owns the land the pool sits on with his siblings, and who has since watched his livelihood wither under the desert sun.

Within days, the pool became a summertime magnet for Israelis, drawing hundreds of visitors a week who traipsed over the Nemers’ land. A lawmaker in Israel’s Parliament on social media promoted visiting the site as an enjoyable means of “occupying the land.”

No one claimed responsibility for cutting the pipe. But Israeli settlers have celebrated the refilling of the pool in videos shared on social media, while one Israeli lawmaker said that “heroic settlers” had returned the pool to “Jewish hands.”

In the West Bank, where water is already limited, settlers have vandalized water and sanitation systems at least 80 times so far this year, according to United Nations data. Settlers have also built illegal outposts close to springs, and then intimidated Palestinians who come to bathe or water their livestock there.

The attacks, which often cut off entire communities from running water for days or even weeks at a time, are part of a surge of settler violence in the West Bank. Over the past three years, extremist settlers have violently driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and set fire to cars, houses and mosques.

Mr. Nemer sought help from the Civil Administration, an Israeli military body overseeing civilian affairs for Palestinians in parts of the West Bank. In a letter to his lawyer in July, viewed by The New York Times, the administration said that the pipeline would be reconnected, but it did not respond to his demand to have the trespassers evicted from his property.

Israeli forces reconnected the pipeline and made “efforts to prevent further damage to the water line,” a military statement said, adding that a fence was erected “to prevent lawbreakers from entering the area.” The military also said that the pool was on private land and that the water diversion was “unauthorized.”

Water did flow back to Mr. Nemer’s fields — but only for a day before it was sabotaged again, he said. On a recent visit to the site, much of it remained unfenced.

“It breaks my heart to see them in our pool,” Mr. Nemer said. He added that he was worried about what would happen if he attempted to reconnect the pipe himself. “I’m afraid that if I go there they will beat me up,” he said.

Settlers from a nearby outpost refused to answer questions about the reservoir.

Some former senior Israeli generals and officials say that Israel’s right-wing government is not doing enough to stop the violence in the West Bank, aimed at ultimately driving most Palestinians out of the territory, which Israel has occupied since 1967.

Most of the people The Times spoke to at the pool said they were Israeli settlers. Many said that knowing the water came at the expense of local Palestinian farms was part of the draw.

“It’s good that this makes life here harder for the Arabs — this country belongs to the people of Israel,” said Ori, 15, a high schooler from Asael, a settlement on the southern edge of the West Bank. “This place is a lot of fun,” he added, sitting with his friends and smoking a hookah pipe.

Israeli flags lined one side of the pool, while a large metal Star of David had been erected on the other. Some Israeli lawmakers are determined to turn the reservoir into a government-run tourist spot and have named the site “Herod’s Pool,” after a Jewish king who ruled the region in the first century B.C. Experts say the pool has never been properly excavated or dated, and its origins remain unclear.

Amichay Eliyahu, Israel’s minister of heritage, said his office would dedicate a million dollars to renovating the site. In a phone interview, he said that “if need be, we could expropriate” the pool and compensate the owners.

A few miles away, Mr. Nemer pulled up old deed documents on his phone that he said showed his grandfather had bought the property, including both fields, the pool and the spring that feeds it, over a century ago.

He also had more recent documents issued by the Israeli Civil Administration that appeared to show recognition of the family’s ownership from the authorities.

Mr. Nemer said the family used to get along well with their Israeli neighbors. In the early 1970s, he and his brother excavated, cleaned and filled the reservoir, he said, welcoming both Israelis and Palestinians to swim in the pool and allowing excess water to flow downhill to irrigate their crops.

The site remained popular for over 15 years, Mr. Nemer said. But after several people drowned there, the family decided in the mid-1990s to drain it, fearing they would be held liable for further accidents.

Then, in 2024, new settlers arrived, Mr. Nemer said, adding that around that time, someone sabotaged his water system. The newcomers spoke to him aggressively, Mr. Nemer said, and one of his workers, Jamal Jarwan, said he had been assaulted that year.

Mr. Jarwan lives on the edge of the Nemers’ property, in a community of about a dozen families.

“They want to kick us out of here,” said one resident, Ayed al-Hayas, 32, referring to the settlers.

A day laborer, Mr. al-Hayas said his family relied on the water for cooking, bathing and livestock. “Without water, there is no life,” he said.

item.title: Holding the Fort in Manhattan to Defy Coup Leaders in Myanmar
item.description:
Half a block from Central Park, on East 77th Street, the fault lines of a faraway conflict run through a sandstone townhouse.

The top two floors of this five-story structure are occupied by officials who answer to Myanmar’s military-backed government. The lower three floors are the purview of a career diplomat who rejects that government as illegitimate.

The diplomat, U Kyaw Moe Tun, arrived in New York in 2020 during the depths of the pandemic as Myanmar’s envoy to the United Nations. A few months later, the elected government that he represented was overthrown by the military. But he has steadfastly refused to work for the generals. His defiance of the military — and his refusal to give up his post at the U.N. and the townhouse, Myanmar’s permanent mission to the U.N. — provides a window into the long, grinding struggle for democracy in Myanmar.

Neither the military-backed officials, who were once Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun’s subordinates, nor his allies ever leave the mission unattended, scared to give the opposing side an opening to change the lock.

“We control the key,” Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun told me during a recent visit to the mission. Of his upstairs neighbors, he said, “They watch what we do. Today, you will be in their reports.”

The U.N. still lists the ousted government as the official head of state. But the military-backed government has increased the pressure on Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun ahead of this week’s meeting of world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly.

On a quest for international legitimacy, the former junta chief, Min Aung Hlaing, has recast himself as the civilian president of Myanmar, rising to the post through elections that were widely derided as a sham. He has since walked down red carpets alongside leaders like Xi Jinping of China, Narendra Modi of India and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

In July, Myanmar’s government sent a letter to the U.N. secretary general, António Guterres, saying Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun had misappropriated $2.6 million in his bid to stay on at the U.N. It also called him a “fugitive,” a “thief” and a “traitor.” This month, it reiterated many of those accusations and said it was in touch with Interpol over the matter.

“This year, there’s an all-out effort,” said Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun, who was dismissed by the junta after it seized power in 2021. Since then, he said, it had voided his passport and had repeatedly tried to freeze the mission’s bank account.

He memorably defied the junta at the U.N. in 2021. In June, he addressed the Security Council, accusing it of “failures to fulfill its mandate” on Myanmar. But as in previous years, Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun does not expect to be speaking before the General Assembly this month.

In 2021, there was an attempt on his life, which led to a monthslong security detail provided by the United States. “I went to Costco in a bulletproof van,” he said about his weekly grocery haul.

His family has also suffered.

The official residence of the ambassador, in upstate New York, was contaminated by lead paint, prompting a public health inspector to advise the family to move out. Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun said that was not possible because the junta would take over the house. The health inspector told him that he was sacrificing his son, who was a toddler at the time. The family stayed, and volunteers from the diaspora helped repaint the walls.

Now 7, the boy still has a speech delay, caused by the lead contamination, said Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun, who also has a teenage daughter.

At the office in the mission, Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun keeps gifts and fan mail from supporters, as well as name tags from various functions, as if to remind himself that he is indeed a representative of Myanmar. A 2020 calendar with a photo of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, the former leader of the country who remains the regime’s prisoner, still adorns a wall.

From here, he regularly has video calls with people back home who are navigating what has turned into one of the world’s most violent conflicts. More than 100,000 people are believed to have been killed and nearly four million displaced by the brutal civil war between pro-democracy forces and the military, which is known to attack civilians as part of its strategy.

“He is the only ambassador the people have left,” said June Su, an aide of his who defected from the Myanmar Embassy in Phnom Penh.

Thaung Hlaing, a retired chauffeur and supporter of Mr. Kyaw Moe Tu’s, has helped with fund-raisers, plus small repair jobs at the mission and the envoy’s residence.

“We want him to be comfortable,” Mr. Thaung Hlaing said. “We help where we can.”

For more than a year after the coup, Mr. Thaung Hlaing spent nights in the mission to keep junta allies from taking it over. These days, younger volunteers are doing that job: one is a doctor, and two others are Uber drivers.

Shortly after the coup in 2021, the chargé d’affaires from the Myanmar Embassy in Washington attempted a physical takeover of the mission but backed down when dozens of diaspora members showed up to protect it, Mr. Thaung Hlaing and other activists said.

When two military-backed diplomats came down the stairs one recent evening, they hurried past Mr. Thaung Hlaing and out the door, avoiding eye contact.

Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun was not always a revolutionary. In the 1990s, seeking a stable job, he joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs when Myanmar was ruled by a different junta.

During his first stint as a young diplomat in New York, he avoided speaking Burmese to his wife in public places popular with Asian communities, scared to raise attention among others from Myanmar. “People were not that happy with us,” he said, referring to the government at the time.

His defense of the Myanmar military’s ethnic cleansing campaign against the Muslim Rohingya minority has drawn scorn. (Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace laureate, has also been criticized for downplaying the violence, which the U.N. and the United States have called a genocide.)

Now, in an attempt to distance himself from that stance, Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun said, “The government had limited leeway to handle it, but they tried their best.”

One of his biggest challenges these days is financial: The funds in the mission’s bank account are dwindling. Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun said he had reduced expenditures to a mere $20 a month. For example, he let go of the gardener and now mows the lawn of his residence himself. He has also stopped paying himself a salary, relying on support from his brother instead.

“I am basically broke,” he said, and laughed.

To save paying overtime to his driver, he now regularly drives himself in the mission’s black Cadillac.

One recent afternoon, he was heading to the U.N. headquarters to prepare to chair a meeting. He pulled out of a parking spot and stopped. “One moment,” he said, getting out to place a white bollard sign in the middle of the spot to hold it.

He was back less than three hours later, but someone had removed the sign and another car was in the space. The mission, however, was still under his control.

]]>
